Yet, the core idea is actually easy to get.
They're trying to build an AI system that can predict how the human brain responds when a person watches something, hears something, or reads something.
That's the whole idea.
For years, neuroscience has mostly studied the brain in pieces.
One group looks at vision, another looks at speech, another looks at faces, motion, emotion, and so on.
That has led to a lot of useful discoveries, but it also means the overall picture is kind of broken up.
What Meta is trying to do with Tribe V2 is build one system that can look across video, audio, and language together and connect that to real brain activity measured through fMRI scans.

And the scale here is serious.
The system was trained on 451.6 hours of fMRI data collected from 25 people across four naturalistic studies, including movies, podcasts, and silent videos.
Then it was evaluated on a much wider pool totaling 1,117.7 hours from 720 people.
That's a lot of brain data.
The model predicts activity across 20,484 cortical points and 8,82 subcortical voxels.

The main pitch here is this.
A lot of AI agents sound smart in chat.
Yet, once you ask them to carry out a real task from start to finish, they lose track, restart, forget what you wanted, or fail the second the situation changes.
GwynClaw is trying to solve exactly that.
The project came out of the open GWN community and instead of chasing the title of most conversational agent, it focuses on execution.
Can the system actually finish the work?
Say you're doing an Excel job and halfway through you change the format, then ask it to remove duplicates, then add a summary, then switch the output again.
A lot of agents treat every change like a brand new request.
Juan Claw is built to keep the whole task alive while those changes happen.
It can pause, reorder, insert, remove, and continue without acting like everything just reset.
A big part of that comes from its memory system, which has three layers.
A stable identity layer, a long-term background layer, and a dynamic trajectory layer.
Basically, it tries to keep your broader context, your working history, and your live task state all at once.

Then it adds something called context slimming, which is really just a smart way of cutting down the junk while keeping the important details that helps the system stay stable over long tasks without drowning in its own context or running up huge tokens costs.
Another smart move is that it doesn't depend on some clean isolated browser demo world.
A lot of agents work nicely in controlled environments and then fall apart the second they hit real websites with loginins, cookies, cached states, and anti-bot systems.
Giwin claw takes over the local browser environment instead, so it can use real login states, cookies, and cached info to operate more like a real user inside actual systems.
And then there's the part that makes it stand out the most.
It's meant to evolve.
Most agents today are basically fixed.
If they fail, you get an error and move on.
If you correct them, they may fix it once, yet they don't truly improve over time.
Juenclaw adds a self-evolution loop where failures and negative user feedback get logged, analyzed for root causes, and turned into targeted improvements.
So, the cycle becomes execution, failure, learning, optimization, and then another attempt.
That means the agent is supposed to get better through repeated real use instead of staying frozen the day it launches.

That was until 1968, when a young physicist working in relative obscurity found a key to unlocking these subatomic secrets.

A shy but technically gifted student, Veneziano had moved to Israel to complete his PhD before taking up a research position at CERN near the Swiss city of Geneva.
Although widely respected, CERN had yet to become the particle physics powerhouse that it is today.
And it would be at CERN, in a small office, that Veneziano stumbled across a formula originally discovered by Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler.
Known as the Euler beta equation, Veneziano plucked it from the annals of 18th century mathematics and applied it to 20th century particle physics.
It was as if he'd stumbled across the chef's secret menu, the guide that, for the first time, revealed exactly how the portion sizes scaled with the ingredients.
What input matched what output.
Veneziano published his paper and then hit it off on a 4-week vacation and, in his own words, did not think much about it.
But by the time he returned, his formula had already become the talk of the town.
And it would be this formula that would turn out to be the founding discovery of string theory.
To the defense, this was beauty in its rawest form.
A centuries-old equation traced perfectly over brand-new data.
Veneziano's equation would become the first exhibit in what would grow into one of the longest running trials in theoretical physics.
Although at the time, no one realized it.
Indeed, as Veneziano later admitted, "I was just looking for a model.
I had no idea it would lead to strings." And so, armed with Veneziano's equation, physicists could finally match the inputs to the outputs.
It was a persuasive piece of evidence, but circumstantial.
They were still no closer to describing what exactly was actually occurring at the point of collision.
They could still not see inside the kitchen, understand why or how all these new particles were created.
The answer to this, however, came sooner than expected.

For in September 1969, mere weeks after the hippie movement reached its cultural crescendo at Woodstock, a radical reinterpretation of Veneziano's idea would come in part from physicist Leonard Susskind, a witness for the defense of string theory we will meet many, many times.
Susskind was born in the New York borough of the Bronx in 1940, a cultural world away from hippie California.
His father was a local plumber working the rotten tenements in and around Harlem.
And after attending college to study heating engineering, Susskind Jr. fell in love with an unlikely muse, theoretical physics.
Eventually, he plucked up the courage to tell his father that he wanted to be a physicist.
"Get out of here.
You ain't going to work in no drug store," came the reply.
"Not a pharmacist, a physicist, like Einstein," Susskind Jr. had clarified.
At the end of the 1960s, Susskind hit upon a new interpretation of Veneziano's work.
In Chicago, the same truth was dawning on Japanese physicist Yoichiro Nambu, and Danish physicist Holger Bech Nielsen also independently had the same light bulb moment.
The trio each realized that the root cause of physicists' problems with colliding protons was that they'd been treating them as point-like particles.
Infinitesimally small specks with no dimensions, much as we still think of electrons today.
Nambu, Nielsen, and Susskind suspected a deeper truth was hiding behind Veneziano's equation.
Protons weren't point-like, they proposed.
One-dimensional ropes that could vibrate in different ways.
Reviewers dismissed it, and the dismissal cut deep.
I felt like I'd gotten hit over the head with a trash can.
I was very, very deeply upset." Susskind would later recall.

According to the new hadronic string theory they had proposed, the mysterious escalating melody of masses inside the Bevatron wasn't a collection of completely different particles, but instead came from the same string vibrating at different frequencies.
Was this the chef's secret recipe?
Was nature cooking with strings?
For a brief moment, physicists, just like the hippies, had elevated themselves to a state of deep enlightenment.
The trouble is, they were wrong.

This unsettling realization came on the back of an experiment taking place less than an hour's drive south of Golden Gate Park, at a completely different type of accelerator to the Bevatron, the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center.
Here, physicists weren't firing protons, they were using them for target practice.
The accelerator center was effectively a high-speed gun shooting electrons down a 2-mile long range.
The hope was that by relentlessly bombarding protons, physicists could finally see what they were made of.
The Bevatron was like a butterfly net hoping to catch whichever strange subatomic creatures fluttered past.
The Stanford Linear Accelerator Center was more like a surgical scalpel slicing open the proton to see what was inside.

If protons were large clouds of charge as had been the assumption, then the incoming electrons shouldn't lose a lot of energy upon collision with their tiny targets and would be scattered off at shallow angles.
Except that's not what physicists saw at the accelerator center.
Instead, electrons lost significant energy and pinged off at surprisingly large angles.
It was as if the electrons were hitting hard substructures within the proton itself.
The idea had already been floating around in the physics ether for half a decade.
In 1964, physicists Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig had proposed that some particles were in turn made of smaller particles, quarks.
Some models worked better with them, but until the experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, it wasn't clear whether quarks were real or mere mathematical sleight of hand.
But it wouldn't take long for physicists to tie the loose ends together.
Within a few years, the proton structure had been neatly bundled into a theory called quantum chromodynamics or QCD.
This theory perfectly explained how protons are made of three quarks bound together by the exchange of particles called gluons.
And so the electrons at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center were pinging off the quarks inside the protons.
Quarks and quantum chromodynamics were a hammer blow for the infant idea of string theory.
In courtroom terms, it was as if the prosecution had landed a devastating cross-examination.
The case for string theory had barely been opened, but now it seemed to slam firmly shut.
Most physicists quietly left the field behind and moved on to other projects.
Only a few hardy souls remained, leaving string theory lifeless but not completely dead.
But those who stayed behind started asking a different question.
What if string theory wasn't just a failed detour in particle physics, but the first clue in a far deeper mystery?
Not just a theory of the subatomic, but a theory of everything.
String theory is a part of 21st century physics that fell by accident into the 20th century.
A pipe rests gently on a scattered pile of dog-eared papers.
Books jut out precariously from the edge of the table.
A single piece of chalk lies expectantly on a ledge beneath the blackboard filled with frantically written equations.
After Albert Einstein died in April 1955, this was the state of his office.
And it was a scene we were never supposed to see.
When Life magazine photographer Ralph Morse heard of the physicist's death, he raced the 90 miles from his home to Princeton.
And after bribing his way in with a bottle of Scotch, Morse was able to photograph Einstein's desk within hours of his death.
But it's what's on the blackboard that's perhaps the most telling.
This was Einstein's final attempt to solve a problem that had become a decades-long obsession.
Einstein was searching for a unified field theory, a single framework that could explain both gravity and the electromagnetic force.
And yet despite 30 years of trying, his holy grail remained agonizingly out of reach.
Someone else would have to step forward, reopen the case, and find what even the great man could not.
By the time string theory appeared at the end of the 1960s, physicists were attempting to do just that.
To tie gravity to not only the electromagnetic force, but to the strong and weak forces, too.
One beautiful, elegant, and coherent theory of everything.
The trouble was, gravity spoke a very different language to the other three fundamental forces.
It is best described by Einstein's own general theory of relativity, and introduces the smooth, continuous fabric of space-time.
A fabric that is warped by objects with mass to provide the illusion of an invisible gravitational pull.
In quantum physics, on the other hand, the language of the other three fundamental forces, electromagnetism and the strong and weak force, this smoothness is jarred.
In the quantum world, everything comes in blocks of fixed, preordained sizes.
The universe it describes is grainy, the very opposite of that described by Einstein in his theory.
These two worlds seemed unresolvably at odds.
Remarkably, however, string theory, despite being bruised and battered by its run-in with quarks and quantum chromodynamics, offered a ray of hope.
A faint glimmer of a theory of everything.
A potential way to explain all four fundamental forces using the same language.
The language of vibrating strings.
Originally, physicists had only considered open strings, those where the ends were free to dangle, like an ordinary piece of rope.
A photon, for example, the particle that carries the electromagnetic force, is represented by a single vibrating string.
The ends of the string represent charged particles.
At one end is the electron, and at the other end is its antimatter partner, a particle called a positron.
The photon string is literally the link between them, explaining the attraction between their opposing electric charges.
When a particle meets its antimatter equivalent, they annihilate one another with their combined masses turning into a flurry of energy.
String theory, therefore, elegantly paints annihilation as the simple act of two string ends meeting.
So far, so straightforward.
But it was only when string theorists started exploring the properties of closed strings, those where the ends joined together to form a continuous loop, that their jaws began to drop.
And to understand the importance of closed strings to a theory of everything, we need to talk about a strange property of subatomic particles called spin.
About a century ago, physicists realized that orbiting subatomic particles, like electrons, behave like they were generating two magnetic fields.
Magnetic fields are created when electric charges move.
So, it followed that if the negatively charged electron has two magnetic fields, then it must be moving in two different ways.
An obvious movement was the electron's orbital motion around the nucleus of an atom.
But physicists wondered whether electrons could also be spinning on the spot.
If true, electrons would be a bit like the Earth, which both spins on its axis and orbits around the Sun.
However, physicists quickly realized their mistake.
In order to generate that magnetic field, electrons would have to be spinning faster than the speed of light.
And of course, that would be impossible.

So while physicists no longer think of subatomic particles as actually spinning, they still use the word spin when it comes to describing the source of that second magnetic field, which turned out to simply be a property of the particle, not something caused by actual spinning.
Different particles have different spin values, and that's what distinguishes the two families of particles from one another.
Fermions such as electrons, quarks, and neutrinos all have spins equal to a half.
By contrast, bosons always have a spin that's equal to a whole number.
The Higgs boson for example has a spin of zero.
Other bosons are responsible for carrying the electromagnetic, weak, and strong forces, and all of them have spins equal to one.
Yet according to string theory, the vibration of a closed string will always represent a particle with a spin equal to two.
And though it may not seem like it, this subtle realization was a landmark moment both in the storied history of string theory and in the entire history of physics itself.
For the defense, this was exhibit A.
Long before string theory, physicists had speculated about a spin-2 particle.
Now it appeared to fall naturally out of closed strings.
The jury surely had to take notice.
And so to hammer home their case, the defense called Soviet physicist Dmitri Blokhintsev to the stand.
Blokhintsev was a big hitter in Soviet society.
Indeed, he once wrote a book on the implications of quantum mechanics that aligned physics with Marxist-Leninist philosophy.
It won him the Stalin Prize in 1952, and 4 years later he was made a Hero of Socialist Labor.
When Blokhintsev died in 1979, his obituary was signed by Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev personally, who lamented that Soviet science has suffered a heavy loss.
And it was in 1934, working alongside Fyodor Kalitzin, that Blokhintsev coined the word graviton to describe a hypothetical particle that would carry the gravitational force.
The other three forces, electromagnetic, weak and strong, can all be neatly explained by the exchange of particles.
These particles have been detected through experiments time and time again, like the photon for the electromagnetic force.
However, no one has ever found a graviton.
This is because the idea of a graviton has deeper problems.
The other three forces and their bosons can all be explained by a set of rules known as a quantum field theory, a type of theory that physicists can use clever tricks to keep stable.
With these other three forces, physicists can mathematically patch up any holes that appear in their theories using a trick called renormalization.
Not so with gravity.
Instead, patching one hole seems to create several more.
Trying to patch those holes creates more still.
In other words, a quantum field theory of gravity, one that contains gravitons, quickly breaks down at very high energies.
Of course, this hasn't stopped physicists from working out just what properties a graviton should have.
First of all, it has to be massless, just like the photon.
The distance over which a force operates, its range, is linked to the mass of the bosons that carry it.
The heavier the boson, the shorter the range.
Gravity, just like the electromagnetic force, has an infinite range, and so gravitons must have a mass of zero.
Gravity also affects all matter in the universe, regardless of other properties such as electrical charge.
And it turns out the only way gravitons would be able to do this is if they are spin-2 particles.
Indeed, this relationship is so sacrosanct that in fact any massless particle with a spin equal to two must behave like a graviton.
And according to string theory, a closed string creates a spin-2 particle.
On paper, that's a graviton.
And it is here that we arrive at the single biggest attraction of string theory, the thing that has seen scores of scientists rally behind it.
The reason billions of dollars have been poured into the field in the decades since, a key pillar of its courtroom defense, and the very idea that saw it resurrected from the dead.
Without even trying, merely by considering what happens if a string forms a closed loop, suddenly one of the most sought-after particles in all of physics pops out of the theory.
It was as if the witness had suddenly confessed before anyone had even posed the question.
And, in the same breath, laid out the rest of the evidence.
A single theory that would be able to predict the existence and properties of the bosons that carry all four fundamental forces, even gravity.
And so, unsurprisingly, this version of string theory came to be known as bosonic string theory.
This was physics at its most beautiful.
And the defense argued that this inherent beauty strengthened the case for bosonic string theory even further.
By treating the graviton as a closed string rather than a point-like particle, the holes in its quantum field theory suddenly could be patched just like the other forces.
There's no runaway chaos that obliterates the theory at high energies.
And to understand this, let's imagine two masses inching ever closer to one another.
Physicists describe gravity using an inverse square law.
This means that every time you halve the distance between the masses, their gravitational attraction quadruples.
As the two masses edge closer and closer together, the attraction between them skyrockets.
And as the gap shrinks to zero, the strength of gravity becomes infinite and the theory breaks down.
But the gap can only shrink to zero if the particles are treated as point-like, with no width, depth, or height.
Bosonic string theory replaces this idea with particles as one-dimensional strings.

And so if gravity works through the exchange of gravitons, and gravitons are closed strings that have a dimension, the two masses can no longer get infinitely close to one another and still be exchanging gravitons.
With no runaway rampage towards infinity, physicists can patch the holes in the theory just as they did with the other three forces.
This was a prime example of beauty offering more than mere decoration.
Instead, it offered salvation.
The elegant geometry of strings vanquishing infinities in a way that point-like particles simply couldn't.
The defense should seize the momentum with a simple, intoxicating idea.
The apparent differences between gravity and its fellow forces could be explained away as the difference between a closed string and an open one.
And at the heart of the matter, the forces were united by a single notion.
Everything is vibrating strings.
If bosonic string theory were correct, it seemed to offer something that even Einstein couldn't muster, a possible path to a theory of everything.
The end of physics as we knew it and the beginning of something far greater.
And yet, if it were that straightforward, physicists wouldn't still be arguing over string theory to this day.
There would be no need to put string theory on trial, no courtroom, no lawyers, and plenty of Nobel prizes.
Every trial begins with opening statements designed to dazzle.
The defense had made its case with elegance and flair.
But now came the cross-examination and the prosecution's evidence was damning.
In physics, as in art, symmetry is a key to beauty.
A large crowd gathers around the tiny computer screen eager to watch the drama unfold.
Suddenly, the message arrives.
It's clear, time-stamped, and intact.
But 3 minutes later, the physicist sends it.
Something has clearly gone wrong, but not with the equipment, with reality.
The message arrived before it was sent, its information traveling backwards in time.
The usually ironclad rules of cause and effect upended entirely.
This unnerving paradox is the kind of thing that happens when you introduce hypothetical particles called tachyons, particles that can travel faster than the speed of light.
Tachyons were a fundamental flaw in bosonic string theory, which bizarrely seemed to predict their existence.
For all its elegance and beauty, bosonic string theory seemed to summon the spectre of superluminal travel.
This was not beauty, but a grotesque gargoyle.
Surely the correct theory of everything couldn't allow this.
And yet tachyons were just the beginning.
The faster-than-light particles turned out to be the least of string theory's problems.
They were merely the first piece of evidence introduced by the prosecution in a long and seemingly watertight rebuttal.
The speed of light as the ultimate cosmic limit is a cornerstone of Einstein's special relativity.
And special relativity rests on an assumption so important that breaking it would be tantamount to physics perjury.
Lorentz invariance is the idea that the laws of physics don't play favorites.
Whether you're drifting in space, sprinting down a corridor, or hurtling past the Earth at 99.9% the speed of light, the rules should remain unchanged.
No observer can have a privileged view of reality.
The speed of light is the same for all observers.
And so strip away Lorentz invariance and reality starts to waver.
Particles might behave differently depending on how fast you're moving.
The whole of physics begins to crumble.
In other words, Lorentz invariance seems non-negotiable.
And yet when string theorists try to apply quantum physics to their elegant strings, the algebra buckled.
Lorentz invariance seemed to collapse.
And that wasn't all.
The prosecution pressed on.
They reminded the jury that in quantum theory, particles can't take on just any value, only certain allowed ones.
Yet when physicists tried to quantize bosonic strings, the math spat out phantom states with negative probabilities.
Probabilities usually live on a scale from zero to one.
Zero means impossible, one means certain.
But bosonic string theory seemed to introduce probabilities below zero.
And a negative probability isn't more impossible, it's nonsensical.
Like betting on a horse with odds of minus one, it just doesn't work.
And so a theory that allows such absurdities is a theory in contempt of court.
The prosecution had landed yet another hammer blow, but they weren't finished.
They were going three for three.
For string theory also failed to reproduce a phenomenon already proven beyond reasonable doubt.
The prosecution now called its star witness, Chien-Shiung Wu.
Wu was born in the Chinese province of Jiangsu in 1912, mere weeks after the sinking of the Titanic.
She'd stay in and listen to the radio instead of playing outside with other children.
Her father would read her passages from scientific journals instead of children's stories.
In 1936, she left China for the United States.
It was a jarring transition.
She looked into attending the University of Michigan, but women weren't even allowed to use the front entrance.
The University of California, Berkeley promised a more liberal life, yet Wu remained culturally adrift and far from home, often finding comfort in meals from a nearby Chinese restaurant.
But scientifically, Wu flourished.
She was recruited into the Manhattan Project and helped develop the atomic bomb.
She later became known as the first lady of physics and in some circles the Chinese Marie Curie.
But her most famous work came in 1956 when she performed a clever intricate experiment to show that the weak force, the one responsible for radioactive decay, violates parity.
To understand parity, imagine a clock reflected in a mirror.
The numbers may be reversed, but the hands still go round in the usual direction from 12 to 3 to 6 to 9.
The reflected clock behaves just like a clock in the real world and so physicists would say that the two clocks exhibit parity.
However, not all the fundamental forces behave this way and it was Wu that proved it.
Wu trapped spinning cobalt nuclei in a magnetic field and waited for some of the neutrons to decay into protons emitting electrons in the process.
The first time she ran the experiment, most of the electrons were emitted downwards.

Look at this reflected in a mirror and you'd see the nuclei spin direction reversed just as the numbers on the clock were, but like the hand on the clock, the direction of the emitted electrons would stay the same.
And so Wu tested this reflection by flipping the orientation of the magnetic field, which sent the nuclei spinning in the opposite direction just as in the mirror image.
Except now, most of the electrons were spat out upwards.
The mirror image did not match what we see in the real world and so the weak force did not obey parity.
Wu found that there was a left and right to fundamental physics.
By the early 1970s, Wu's result wasn't in question.
Parity violation had long been written into the rules of physics, proven time and time again.
And yet once again, bosonic string theory, for all its elegance and potential as a theory of everything, simply couldn't account for it.
It was yet another gaping hole in the defense's testimony.
Here the contradiction at the heart of string theory was laid bare.
Sometimes it wasn't beautiful enough, spawning hideous tachyons.
Other times it was too beautiful, unable to accommodate the messy asymmetries of the real world, like parity violation.
Beauty, it seemed, could cut both ways.
Tachyons, impossible ghosts, non-Lorentz invariance or parity violation.
Any one of these would be enough to consign a theory to the dustbin of history.
And yet string theory, physics' perennial survivor, squirmed and wriggled its way out of all of them.
Cornered and battered, the defense turned to an unlikely savior.
English physicist Claude Lovelace.
Lovelace was a paid-up member of the eccentric physicist club.
Known to be a bit of a loner, he would often avoid major conferences, yet still sent in important scientific papers.
In later life, Lovelace filled his home with parakeets and thousands of classical music CDs.
The unusual combination helped him think.
Somehow Lovelace had managed to become a physics professor without ever obtaining a PhD.
He started one in London, but dropped out before completing it.
That doesn't seem to have held him back.
For 1971, Lovelace made a fundamental, but often overlooked, contribution to string theory.
He argued that the universe has hidden dimensions, secret locked rooms the defense urged the jury to imagine.
Evidence concealed from view, but essential to their case.
The world around us seems to be four-dimensional.
There are the three spatial dimensions, left, right, up, down, front, back.
Then, the one dimension of time.
In other words, we always need four numbers to accurately describe an object's location.
Three for where it is, and another one for when it is.
However, Lovelace wondered what would happen if vibrating quantum strings didn't have to be confined to our four-dimensional world.
And slowly, but surely, he ramped up the number of dimensions.
First five, then six, seven, eight, nine.
Eventually, at a total of 26 dimensions, 25 space and one time, string theory seemed to stabilize.
Others, including Holger Bech Nielsen, ran with the idea, proving that it both eliminated the probabilistic ghosts and maintained Lorentzian invariance.
Born in Copenhagen in 1941, Nielsen was another of physics eccentrics.

The unkempt hair, the ever-present bow tie, and indeed, back in the earliest days of string theory, it had been Nielsen who, alongside Nambu and Susskind, had realized that Veneziano's work implied strings.
Unfiltered and unpredictable, perhaps Lovelace's and Nielsen's maverick nature was just what was needed to open up the extra dimensions.
String theory was suddenly on slightly stronger footing.
The defense lawyers were regaining ground.
But this newfound stability involved a massive trade-off, one that the prosecution will seize upon to undermine the case for string theory time and time again.
In order to explain things we have a lot of evidence for normal probabilities and the Lorentz invariance, string theory would have to invent 22 additional dimensions that we have no evidence for.
And even then, this sprawling mega-dimensional reality can't solve all of string theory's problems.
Time-traveling tachyons were still center stage, and the lack of parity violation remained a gaping hole in the theory.
But there were answers to be found there, too.
The defense calls for its own star witness, Yuri Golfand.
Golfand was born in 1922 in Kharkiv, which today is Ukraine's second largest city.
Even from an early age, he showed precocious talent.
He started playing chess with his father age just four, and soon became the better player.
Underscoring the impact he would have both on physics and the people around him, fellow physicist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Andrei Sakharov once called Golfand a Mozart of physics.
Picture a chessboard, like the one Golfand spent so much time playing on as a boy.
A chessboard has 64 squares, divided equally between black and white.
In other words, for every white square, there is a corresponding black square.
In this way, a chessboard has an underlying symmetry.
In 1971, Golfand became one of the first proposed that the subatomic world exhibits a similar kind of symmetry.
Just as every black square on a chessboard has a corresponding white square, so, suggested Golfand, every boson has a corresponding fermion, and vice versa.
To name the supersymmetric partner of a fermion, you simply add an S before it.
So, charmingly, the partner of a quark is a squark, an electron is paired with a selectron, and neutrinos are matched to sneutrinos.
Indeed, laser strength theory pioneer John Schwarz once quipped that he wasn't responsible for this language.
However, the supersymmetric partners of bosons are named slightly differently, simply by adding an -ino to the end.
So, the famous Higgs boson has a partner that sounds a little bit like a magician, the stupendous Higgsino.
Though in practice, physicists often bend the rules.
Hence, names like gluino for the fermionic partner of the gluon.
Although to this day, no supersymmetric particles have yet been found, an absence that the prosecution will pounce upon later in the case.
And so, at the start of the 1970s, several other physicists were also dabbling with similar ideas.
Eventually, they combined supersymmetry with Lovelace's 26-dimensional version of bosonic string theory, and superstring theory was born.
Initial results were promising.
This new theory could now account for fermions as well as bosons.
The inclusion of fermions could see off the parity issue, providing a way for it to be violated.
It also did away with those pesky tachyons.
No faster-than-light travel, no effect preceding cause.
What's more, the number of spatial dimensions came crashing down from Lovelace's unruly 25 to a slightly more manageable nine.
And so, having been on the ropes for much of the prosecution's cross-examination, the defense team had rallied.
For each of the major issues with the original bosonic string theory, superstring theory now provided an alibi.
What had looked like a lost cause had yet again surged back to life.
Beauty had become the compass once more, pointing towards a hidden country where string problems seemed to dissolve into the mist.
But that wasn't the end.
For the prosecution were forced to pivot, honing in on a new line of attack, and not an unreasonable one.
If these extra dimensions exist, why can't we see them?
Six extra dimensions that we had no evidence for were hardly more credible to the jury than 22.
And so for string theory's case to remain stable, string theorists desperately needed an answer to a very basic question.
If these extra dimensions really did exist, where were they?
Why, you may ask, do the string theorists insist that space is nine-dimensional?
Simply because string theory doesn't make sense in any other kind of space.
Theodor Kaluza stands on the edge of the water, ready to prove a point.
Now in his 30s, the polyglot theoretical physicist never learned to swim as a child.
But who needs practice when you have books and theories?
Kaluza has recently swotted up on how to swim in the pages of a manual.
And upon entering the water, he duly swims at his first attempt.
A triumph for the theoretical over the practical.
Kaluza's mind was certainly a fertile one.
He could speak at least 15 languages, and liked literature and philosophy almost as much as mathematics and physics.
And like many physicists before and since, Kaluza became transfixed with the idea of unification.
Just as medieval kings would try to unite their respective kingdoms through key and strategic marriages, physicists try to do the same with theories.
Why have two different theories when a single combined theory could suffice?
Kaluza's big idea was to seek a matrimonial bond between Einstein's general theory of relativity and the rules of electromagnetism.
A love match between gravity and light.
The obstacle to such wedded bliss is that the mathematics of each of the theories is fundamentally incompatible with the other.
As we've seen before, the equations explode in a fit of infinities.
And yet in a 1921 paper, Kaluza was able to get them to gel under one condition, that the universe had five dimensions, one more than the four we are used to.
Kaluza was clearly excited by the benefit of adding an extra dimension of space, writing in his paper that it could not amount to the mere alluring play of a capricious accident.
And indeed, when he wrote to Einstein, the great man was more than encouraging.
The idea of achieving this through a five-dimensional world has never occurred to me and is probably new.
I like your idea immensely.

But of course, as with any attempt to explain the world through extra dimensions, the fact that we don't experience more than four dimensions in our everyday lives was the proverbial elephant in the room.
If Kaluza's extra dimension really did exist, where exactly was it?
A potential answer would come from Swedish physicist Oskar Klein.
The son of Stockholm's first rabbi, Klein became enchanted with science at an early age.
Years later, he would recount the time when he borrowed his mother's opera glasses and used them to stare up at the stars.
Working his way through school university, Klein ended up studying chemistry before pivoting to physics.
And independently to Kaluza, he came up with the idea of a five-dimensional universe.
However, this time offering up an explanation for why we don't see this mysterious fifth dimension.
It is, Klein argued, curled up incredibly small.
On the order of the Planck length.
The smallest meaningful distance in the universe.
When we think of truly small things in physics, one of the first objects that comes to mind is the atom.
Indeed, a typical atom is just a tenth of a nanometer across.
You'd need to line up 150 million atoms side by side in order to match the width of one of your fingernails.
Small, but not small enough.
For the Planck length is 16 trillion trillion times smaller still.
In fact, the Planck length is to the width of an atom what the width of an atom is to the size of the entire solar system.
In the language of physicists, the extra dimension in Kaluza-Klein theory is compactified.
In other words, it is so vanishingly small that we can't see it.
And to see how this works in practice, imagine an ant crawling along the branch of a tree.
From some distance away, the tree looks flat and two-dimensional, as if painted on some far-off canvas.
But the ant knows the truth.
There's a third dimension, and safe in this knowledge, it can happily crawl around the circumference of the branch.

In the same way, our universe would look four-dimensional from up here on the scale of plants, people, and planets, but there could be compactified, curled up dimensions languishing in the hidden depths of reality.

Despite receiving a warm reception from several towering figures of the time, Kaluza-Klein's insights were largely consigned to a mere footnote in the history of early 20th century physics until string theory once more summoned the spectre of hidden dimensions in the 1970s.
By the start of the 1980s, superstring theories predicted the existence of no fewer than six extra spatial dimensions.
The prosecution was circling.
With the tachyon problem subdued and supersymmetry now on life support, string theory still had to answer for the six extra spatial dimensions that stubbornly refused to show themselves.
The court was losing patience.

On the screen, a decades worth of data reduced to dots and lines.
What he is about to reveal would later win him a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Yet in the courtroom of theoretical physics, this was a hostile witness, one summoned from a completely different field with no loyalty to string theory.
And the evidence Perlmutter presented would leave the defense scrambling and hand the prosecution an explosive new line of attack.
The vast majority of astronomers and cosmologists accept that the universe began in an event known as the Big Bang nearly 14 billion years ago.
It started out unimaginably small, far tinier than an atom, and has been expanding ever since, ballooning into the cosmos we see today.
But by now, many eons later, that expansion should be slowing down.
The gravitational pull of all the stuff in the universe, stars, gas, galaxies, dark matter, ought to be applying the brakes.
And in the mid-1990s, as the second superstring revolution roiled through theoretical physics, two teams of astronomers had been busy trying to confirm that deceleration.
It was supposed to just be a routine check.
But when Perlmutter announced his team's results at that press conference in early 1998, they stunned the astronomical community.
For string theorists, it was a bombshell in open court, a line of evidence they hadn't anticipated, and one they had no ready answer for.
Both teams have been using exploding stars called type 1A supernovae to track the expansion history of the universe.
These cosmic detonations occur in binary systems where a dead, dense white dwarf orbits alongside an ordinary star.
Over time, the white dwarf's gravity siphons material from its companion, slowly growing heavier.
But its appetite has a hard limit.
Once the white dwarf nears a critical mass, about 1.4 times that of the sun, known as the Chandrasekhar limit, it becomes unstable.
A wave of thermonuclear reactions rips through it and the star is blown apart.
But what makes type 1A supernovae so useful is that they all explode with roughly the same amount of fuel.
That means they all shine with roughly the same intrinsic brightness.
Astronomers call them standard candles and by comparing how bright they appear to how bright they should be, they can determine their distance.
The dimmest are the furthest away.
Except the two rival teams, Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project and the High-Z Supernova Search Team, both found something deeply unexpected.
The distant supernovae were too dim.
Not just farther than expected, but as if space had expanded more than it should have since their light began its journey towards us.
And the only explanation was shocking.
The expansion of the universe wasn't slowing down.
It was speeding up.
Even today, astronomers have no definitive answer as to why this is happening.
The accelerating expansion is usually put down to something called dark energy, a shadowy entity whose potency only grows as the universe ages.
What dark energy actually is, however, remains, well, dark.
But what we do know is that dark energy implies something about a term in Einstein's equations, the cosmological constant, usually denoted by the Greek letter lambda.
Einstein originally introduced it as a mathematical fix to hold the universe still.
And when Edwin Hubble discovered the universe was actually expanding, Einstein realized his error.
But lambda wasn't a mistake after all.
Today, it's clear that the cosmological constant, the amount of energy that occupies all of empty space, or something acting like that, is real, and it's driving the acceleration.
And more than just setting space's expansion rate, lambda also affects its geometry.
If this energy is negative, the universe has negative curvature.
And if it's positive, as the supernova data seem to suggest, the universe has positive curvature.
And this was and is a big problem for string theory.
We've seen a negative curvature before.
When Polchinski stacked D3 branes in our holographic library, the mass and charge of the branes warped the space, curving the library walls inwards.
Indeed, that's anti-de Sitter, ADS, geometry with negative curvature.
But now, a fundamental cosmological measurement was telling us that the real universe curves the other way.
The walls don't cave in.
In geometric terms, we didn't live in an anti-de Sitter space with negative curvature, but in a de Sitter-like universe, where the curvature is positive, and the expansion accelerates indefinitely.
And that's not merely a mismatch, it strikes at the heart of the most mathematically mature part of M-theory.
AdS/CFT, for all its evidence, turned out to be built on a geometry that clearly clashes with astronomical observations.
Speaking in 2001, Ed Witten said, "I don't know of any clear way to get to sitter space from string theory or M-theory." This was a damning admission from string theory's biggest star witness.
The defense was once again on the ropes.
With no explanation for dark energy, the prosecution smelt blood.
And though what followed wasn't a knockout blow, it might be the defense's last chance to stay on its feet.
Desperate, the defense team called Renata Kallosh to the stand.
Kallosh was born in 1943 in the culturally rich city of Chernivtsi, now part of Ukraine, amid the upheaval of World War II.
She came of age during the Khrushchev thaw, a period of relative openness and reform following Stalin's death.
Against this backdrop, Kallosh moved to Moscow to study physics.
And by 1968, she'd earned her PhD from the capital's prestigious Lebedev Physical Institute.
She would also find love there.
Seminars on cosmological phase transitions are typically known as hotbeds of romance, but it was during one such seminar that she caught the eye of fellow physicist Andrei Linde.
They began talking about physics, and 2 years later they met again, this time at Lake Ladoga near St.
"When I was leaving Ladoga, I kept Renata's hand in mine just a second longer than I was supposed to," Linde recalls.
"A few months later, we were married." The couple recently celebrated their golden wedding anniversary.
Kallosh and Linde quickly became a physics power couple.

As the Soviet Union began to collapse, they left together, first for CERN, and then in 1990 to accept joint professorships at Stanford University, home to one of the world's leading centers for cosmology and theoretical physics.
And they were still at Stanford in 2003 when they helped develop an idea that might rescue string theory from the existential quagmire brought on by the discovery of dark energy.
Working alongside Shamit Kachru and Sandip Trivedi, they devised what became known as the KKLT mechanism, a moniker formed from the initials of their surnames.
Back in the 1980s, amid the first superstring revolution, physicists had made headway in curling up the extra dimensions of string theory.
The work of Calabi and Yau offered a way to fold the origami of the universe into intricate, compact shapes known as Calabi-Yau manifolds.
But even by the early 21st century, this approach faced a serious problem.
The folds weren't stable.
The size and shape of these extra dimensions could fluctuate wildly, leading to universes that were either unstable or unrecognizable.
And so, like the Green-Schwarz mechanism before it, the KKLT mechanism was a patch, a fix for a deeper flaw.
First, it introduced fluxes, fields that thread through the folds of the extra dimensions, acting like invisible tape to hold the shape in place and prevent it from warping.
But that alone wasn't enough.
These solutions still tended to produce universes with negative curvature, anti-de Sitter space.
And so, to fix this, KKLT introduced anti-branes, objects with the opposite energy and charge to regular D-branes.
Adding them tips the balance, finally producing a universe with positive curvature, just like the de Sitter space implied by the supernova results.
But, it turned out that there were a lot of ways to add fluxes and anti-branes to Calabi-Yau manifolds.
Each one produces a different version of string theory, resulting in a different version of the universe with its own laws of physics, particles, and forces.
And this vast expanse of possibilities is known as the string theory landscape.
But this landscape doesn't contain just a handful of different string theories, or even a thousand, not even a million, billion, or trillion different ways, but at least 100 quindecillion.
That's a one followed by 500 zeros.
It's hard to do justice to just how big a number that is.
Compared to these 10 to 500 possible universes, the number of galaxies, stars, or even seconds since the Big Bang are mere rounding errors.
Jacob Bekenstein once calculated the limit of how much information can be stored in a given region of space.
And so if the entire observable universe were a cosmic hard drive, it could hold around 10 to the power of 122 bits of information.
So adding the KKLT mechanism suddenly gave us possible versions of string theory than there is information available in the entire universe to list them.
No matter how smart we are, no matter the size of the computers we build, we can't ever hope to catalog, simulate, or analyze them all, even in principle.
The computational and physical limits of the universe make that utterly impossible.
And so if string theory had been accused of untestability before, it was now, in the eyes of its critics, irreparably so.
To the prosecution, the defense had exchanged uniqueness for a wilderness of alibis.
One such critic, Lee Smolin, didn't mince his words.
If an attempt to construct a unique theory of nature leads to 10 to the power of 500 theories, that approach has been reduced to absurdity.
The defense argued that this is simply what frontier physics looks like, messy, abstract, and occasionally lost in its own beauty.
The prosecution, however, saw something very different, a theory not grounded in evidence, but permanently insulated from it.
And so, if string theory's defense team were to stop the judge and jury throwing out the case for good, they had some key blanks to fill in.
If the universe is accelerating, not just coasting, but racing away from itself, then we're dealing with something far stranger than anyone had planned for.
Instead of a small tweak to the cosmic script, it was a complete rewrite of the opening scene.
The trial was no longer just about strings or particles.

With so many possibilities now on the table, the courtroom had become something else entirely, a grand inquest into not just how the universe exists, but why this particular version of it emerged from the vastness of possibility.
And whatever the answer was, it wouldn't be local.
It wouldn't be small, and it certainly wouldn't leave the early universe untouched.
The great tragedy of science, the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact.
The sun rises slowly over a picture of serenity, a glassy pond with not a ripple to be seen.
A cool early morning mist clings to the calm waters as dragonflies dance between the reeds, the silence only broken by the occasional chirp of a cricket or croak of a frog.
Though it may not seem like it, this picturesque pond shares a lot in common with the modern universe.
It's seemingly calm, balanced, and most importantly, self-contained.
Indeed, according to the theory of the Big Bang, this cosmic pond grew from a tiny puddle about 14 billion years ago.
But like any seemingly still pond, you'd expect to find disturbances beneath the surface, eddies, whirlpools, and currents.
Yet instead of this, the more physicists studied the universe, the more unsettlingly still it became.
The deeper they looked, the more uncanny the calm.
And so in a sense, it wasn't what they saw that was alarming.
It was what they didn't see.
To begin with, there was the flatness problem.
Just like the surface of the serene pond, space today appears to be very close to what astronomers call flat.
In other words, it has almost no curvature at all.
Any tiny deviation from flatness early on should have become exaggerated as space expanded, warping the surface into something visibly bent today.
And yet instead, it's astonishingly smooth.
At first glance, there are two possible explanations for this.
Perhaps space was perfectly flat to begin with, and so simply stayed that way as it grew.
A serene puddle growing into a serene pond.
But the odds of that happening by chance are astronomically low.
The second option is that the pond ballooned so enormously that any initial ripples were ironed out, flattened by sheer size.
But the standard Big Bang model doesn't allow for nearly enough expansion to do the job.
And then, there's the horizon problem.
Even though the pond is now vast, too wide for a ripple to have crossed from one bank to the other since it formed, the entire surface looks perfectly coordinated.
No currents, no temperature differences, every part of the pond seems to have agreed on the same conditions.
And that shouldn't be possible.
For one side of a system to know about the other, to equalize, synchronize, or share information, something has to travel between them.
A ripple, a current, a message in a bottle, something.
But in our expanding pond, there simply hasn't been time for that.
The banks are too far apart.
There hasn't been enough time for ripples or information to reach from one side to the other, for everything to even out.
The speed of light simply isn't fast enough to cover the distance in the time the universe has existed, and yet its opposite sides still appear identical.
And finally, there's the monopole problem.
Predicted particles that, like mythical leviathans lurking in the deep, should be swimming through the cosmos in droves.
Magnetic poles without a partner, a south without a north, a north without a south.
Theories that try to unify the three non-gravitational forces suggest that at high energies, the early universe should have produced huge numbers of them.
And yet, we've never seen one.
That's a serious problem for any theory aiming to describe physics at the highest energies, string theory included.
And so, each of these three problems alone was troubling.
The three of them together was damning.
The Big Bang was our best model of the early universe, but it was leaking at the seams.
If no solution could be found, it might have to be abandoned altogether.
And if even the Big Bang couldn't be trusted, how could grander frameworks like superstring theory, which sought to unify all of physics, hope to succeed?
Luckily for superstring and the Big Bang theory, one man had a single idea that could patch every leak at once.
The court to call is Alan Guth to the stand.
Born in 1947 in New Brunswick, New Jersey, Guth skipped his senior year of high school and enrolled at MIT at just 17, earning a bachelor's, master's, and a PhD all in quick succession.
He began his career in particle physics studying quarks before shifting his focus to cosmology in the mid-1970s, drawn by puzzles like magnetic monopoles and the flatness of space.
Yet Guth struggled and went from temporary post to temporary post until late one night in December 1979, he experienced what he described at the time as a spectacular realization.
Guth figured out the period of rapid exponential expansion could solve not one, but all three Big Bang problems.
And by 1981, he had formally proposed what we now know as cosmic inflation, and his career, understandably, took off.
Inflation is like an underground pipe beneath the pond.
It provides a sort of pressure surge that for the briefest moment blasts huge quantities of water in from below.
The puddle doesn't just grow, it erupts.
Then, the pipe shuts off, leaving the pond to expand at a slower, steadier pace.

According to the theory, this initial inflationary phase saw the universe's size skyrocket from considerably smaller than an atom to about the size of a grapefruit in just a trillionth of a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, doubling in size roughly 80 times.
That may not sound like much, but by the end of inflation, the universe was roughly 10 to the power of 78 times bigger than it had been at the start.
To put that number into context, imagine taking an ordinary shipping container and then expanding it by the same amount.
Suddenly, it would be larger than the entire observable universe.
But how did this relatively straightforward addition solve all the problems of the Big Bang?
Well, the flatness problem hinged on the fact that there hadn't been enough expansion since the Big Bang to smooth out any initial wrinkles.
But inflation adds in the extra required expansion.
Similarly, the horizon problem argued that there hasn't been enough time for ripples to travel between every part of the pond.
Add in the extra expansion from inflation, and suddenly the puddle can start much smaller, much more interconnected, and still be capable of becoming the enormous pond we see today.
And finally, what about the missing monopoles?
Well, inflation solves that, too.

If monopoles were formed in the early universe, they would have been diluted by inflation's vast expansion of space, stretched so thinly across the cosmic pond that we'd expect to find hardly any at all.
At first, inflation looked like a miracle cure.
It fixed the flatness and horizon problems, and even swept the monopoles under the cosmic rug.
The Guth's original idea, although highly elegant in theory, didn't quite work in practice.
His version of inflation ended too violently, leaving behind a universe riddled with bubbles.
And so, as it happened many times before in physics, Guth's original model was beautiful, but when pressed, it cracked under cross-examination.
The defense would need a smoother, more controlled version of the same idea.
And that refinement would one day dramatically intersect with the world of string theory, and it came from a familiar face, Andrei Linde.
Guth's inflation research was too abrupt, like the underground pipe had burst.
Linde added the equivalent of a pressure valve.
The water still rushed in, expanding the pond dramatically, but now in a smoother, more controlled fashion.
The surface could stay calm, coherent.
And that wasn't the end of it.
For Linde's version, the valve didn't simply shut off all at once.
One region of the pond might stop swelling and begin settling, but others could keep expanding.
Some of those regions would even spawn new valves of their own, launching entirely new ponds.
And this process would never end.
Our serene pond, just one amongst countless others, each with its own currents and contours, shaped by the exact circumstances of its birth.
In other words, a vast and expansive landscape of ponds, with each one having its own particles, fundamental forces, and laws of physics.
If this idea sounds familiar, it should.
It's an eerie parallel of the string theory landscape.
And so, here was a completely separate theory, one born from an entirely different perspective, arriving at the same unsettling conclusion.
A vast multitude of universes, each with its own unique physics fingerprint.
Fixing the Big Bang theory suddenly brought it into closer alignment with superstring theory.
The defense's case began to glisten.
But, just as the two theories seem to be converging into something grander, deeper questions began to bubble up.
Could these lush ponds, so elegantly imagined, be nothing more than mirages?
To answer this question, the court summons Cumrun Vafa.
Vafa was born in 1960 in Tehran, the capital of Iran, during a period of profound political turbulence.
The Shah was in the midst of a sweeping modernization campaign known as the White Revolution.
When Vafa was four, Ayatollah Khomeini, a fierce critic of the Shah's reforms, was exiled.
That same year, the Iranian Prime Minister was assassinated in the street.
And so with all of this happening around him, the young Vafa turned his eyes a little higher, to the moon.
"Whenever I would look at the moon, it was bothering me as to why it wouldn't fall to the ground." He would later recall.

"That fact stuck with me, and also why other people were not bothered by it, and treated it as if it were irrelevant." These musings would kick-start a lifelong love affair with the biggest questions about our universe.
This ensuing quest for answers took Vafa first to MIT, then to Princeton, where he completed his PhD in 1985 under the watchful eye of Ed Witten.
And by 2008, he'd made such important contributions to string theory that he was awarded the prestigious Dirac Medal alongside Juan Maldacena and Joseph Polchinski.
And arguably Vafa's most provocative insight had come 3 years before, in 2005.
A sharp, unsettling idea that threatened to throw both string theory and inflationary cosmology into disarray.
Welcome to the swampland.
Vafa looked out across the seemingly boundless landscape of inflationary ponds, each one a possible universe with its own shape and physics, and asked a simple question.
Were any of them actually compatible with string theory?
And in case after case, the answer came back a resounding no.
No matter how you tweak the geometry or rearrange the ingredients, these pond-like universes refused to form.
Or worse, they emerged only by violating principles string theory seems to uphold everywhere else, like how forces should behave or how light particles can be.
In other words, not every mathematically consistent pond is actually physically viable.
Some of them may look placid and still, but step in and you'll find yourself sinking deep into the mud.
What had seemed like a serene pond turns out to be a slurried, stinking mess.
Together, these boggy outcrops make up Vafa's swampland.
A murky, unstable region of the inflationary landscape that cannot be derived from string theory, no matter how hard you try.
Swampland had serious teeth.
Vafa's conjectures aren't proven, but they function like legal precedent, setting the boundaries any defense must reckon with.
And so what once seemed like safe theoretical ground was suddenly treacherous.
Vafa wasn't just surveying the landscape, he was issuing injunctions.
Entire regions were now off-limits.
Vafa and others now began deriving specific mathematical tripwires, constraints that any viable universe must avoid.
Many existing theories stumbled right into them.
One of the biggest casualties was Kallosh-Linde's KKLT team mechanism.
Most known KKLT-type solutions sit squarely in Vafa's swampland.
This is a massive problem for string theorists because they need the KKLT mechanism to stabilize the theory and make it compatible with the accelerating expansion of the universe.
And indeed, Vafa's tripwires also entangle the theory of inflation itself.
In particular, they hit slow-roll inflation hard, the gentle controlled expansion described by Linde.
According to the swampland criteria, the conditions needed for such a smooth and steady growth may simply not be allowed.
The process unfolds too slowly or stretches too far or relies on a kind of delicate balance that string theory seems unwilling to permit.
For critics, this was damning.
String theory couldn't comfortably accommodate the best-known explanations for either dark energy or inflation.

If the swampland conjectures are right, then two of the most widely accepted pillars of modern cosmology are mutually incompatible with string theory, not flawed approximations, fundamentally incompatible.
Although inflation does at least have one advantage over KKLT, it might be testable.
One of the most promising tests comes in the form of primordial gravitational waves.
Inflation should have left its mark either through subtle distortions in the light leftover from the Big Bang or as faint waves still traveling through the universe today.
And several experiments are hunting for them.
Ground-based observatories like BICEP and the Simons Observatory scan the sky for signatures in the leftover light.
Soon, a space-based mission will join the chase.

LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, scheduled for launch in the 2030s, LISA will be the first gravitational wave observatory in space, exquisitely sensitive to low-frequency waves the ground-based detectors can't catch.
If LISA does see the right kind of background signal, it could offer direct evidence that inflation really did shake the universe into being.
But of course, even this wouldn't resolve the deeper question.
For proving inflation shaped our pond is one thing, but proving it filled a multiverse of ponds is quite another.
Eternal inflation may be compelling, but it remains difficult, maybe impossible, to falsify.
Indeed, critics have long warned that it risks slipping from science into metaphysics.
Paul Steinhardt, one of the original architects of inflation, has since become one of its most vocal detractors.
He now argues that inflation has become a self-justifying idea, impossible to rule out and ever more baroque in its defense.
It's the same criticism we've seen thrown at string theory time and time again.
And so, we reach an impasse.
Inflation may be right, but it's slippery.
KKLT may be beautiful, but it's inadmissible.
The case had grown enormous, a legal skyscraper of claims and counterclaims.
But at its foundation sat one quiet, unproven assumption, supersymmetry.
Indeed, the entire defense rested on it.
After all, there could be no superstring theory without supersymmetry.
And yet now, after decades, the court was finally ready to test it.
Supersymmetry is the distinctive prediction of string theory that is most likely to be discovered experimentally.
The sprawling ice sheets of Antarctica are a white, bleak wasteland.
There is nothing for miles save for snowstorms and blizzards.
Yet, as we converge on the geographic South Pole, human-made castles rise above the permafrost.
For here, on the high plateau of Antarctica, some 2,835 m above sea level, is the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.
And among the dozens of buildings that dominate the otherwise desolate landscape is IceCube, a state-of-the-art neutrino observatory.
And yet, the truly impressive part of IceCube is found underground.
In 2005, the very same year Cumrun Vafa went public with Swampland, engineers began using drilling towers and warm water hoses to bore deep holes into the Antarctic ice.
Into each, they lowered long strings with detectors hanging on the ends.
The harsh conditions and inhospitable winters, where the sun doesn't rise for months on end, meant IceCube took five long years to complete.
Thousands of sensors were spread over a cubic kilometer of ice, making it the largest neutrino telescope in the world.
And indeed, IceCube's bread and butter is high-energy neutrinos, produced by calamitous events in the deep, far-off universe.
And yet, it also has its subterranean eyes set a little closer to home.
For IceCube is on the lookout for neutrinos being hurled up from the core of the Earth.
Neutrinos produced by dark matter.
If dark energy had been an agonizing thorn in string theory's side, dark matter might yet prove a powerful ally.
As we've seen already, dark energy is the mysterious entity that appears to be accelerating the universe's expansion.
Dark matter, however, in a sense plays the opposite role.
It is the invisible glue that binds cosmic structures together.
Astronomers first noticed dark matter's effects as far back as the 1930s.
Galaxies within clusters seem to be moving too fast, and one way to explain why these clusters didn't simply fly apart is if there was hidden material inside exerting an extra gravitational pull.
Indeed, individual galaxies told a similar story.
Stars on their edges orbited faster than expected.
Perhaps, astronomers mused, they too were held in place by some invisible adhesive.
At first, though, scientists were stumped as to what dark matter could be made of.
The culprit seemed to have two properties.
It must have mass, otherwise it wouldn't exert gravity, and it must not interact with the light, otherwise we'd see it.
Unfortunately, no suspect in the standard model lineup matched that particular fit.
And so, they wondered, could dark matter be lurking beyond the standard model.
Astronomers interest in dark matter accelerated in the 1970s, just as string theorists were beginning to juggle with supersymmetry.
And it turned out that the lightest supersymmetric particle, the neutralino, would behave just like dark matter.
It is a form of weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP for short.
And from that moment to this, the search for WIMPs gathered pace.
And so it seemed that supersymmetry didn't just streamline string theory, it also seemed to predict one of the most fundamental aspects of our universe.
Finding WIMPs, therefore, would be a ringing endorsement of supersymmetry and bolster the case for string theory, to boot.
And indeed, despite all its promise with dark matter, supersymmetry also had an older alibi.
After all, it was supersymmetry that first let string theory smuggle gravity into quantum mechanics.
Without it, string theory's cleanest prediction, the graviton, vanishes.
And without the graviton, the whole defense begins to unravel at a precipitous pace.
And so string theorists pinned their hopes on the detectors hidden beneath the ice.
If the galaxy is indeed flooded with WIMPs, the solar system should be plunging through them as it orbits around the Milky Way.
Dark matter particles should continually sink into the core of the Earth, where they would collide with one another and produce neutrinos.
Neutrinos that IceCube has been looking for.
Simple enough, except for the fact it hasn't seen any.
Indeed, a study released in early 2025 trolled through a decade of IceCube data and found absolutely no signatures of dark matter coming from the center of the Earth.
Perhaps scientists thought another team would have more luck.
This time with an experiment not tucked away under the Antarctic ice, but hidden a mile underneath South Dakota in an abandoned gold mine.
Except once again, the search here with the LUX Zeppelin experiment also came up short.
But perhaps the heady maelstrom of the galactic center, where stars and dust are constantly swirling around a gargantuan supermassive black hole, offers more positivity for WIMPs.
Indeed, another experiment has been scouring this region for clues.
The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, bolted to the side of the International Space Station, AMS-02 is a hulking $2 billion cosmic ray detector.
Since 2011, it's been measuring high-energy particles that might be produced by WIMP annihilations near the galactic center.
And initial results looked promising.
AMS-02 found more positrons than expected, raising hopes that dark matter might be the culprit.
But again, the signal proved ambiguous.
Pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars, could produce the same excess.
This means that more than a decade on, physicists are still debating what, if anything, AMS-02 has seen.
And so, the result is frustratingly familiar.
Hints, suggestions, and shadows, but never certainty.
The evidence for supersymmetry through dark matter searches remains agonizingly elusive.
But, there is another way.
The most direct tests of supersymmetry have taken place at the largest energies achievable on Earth, at the Large Hadron Collider.
Here, beneath the French-Swiss border, protons are smashed together at near light speeds in the hope that something entirely new might emerge.
If super symmetric particles exist, some should be within the Large Hadron Collider's reach.
The LHC first turned on to much fanfare towards the end of 2008, and within 4 years it made headlines around the world when physicists discovered the Higgs boson, the much lauded god particle.
The Higgs boson and the associated Higgs field is what gives other particles mass.
And yet the discovery of the Higgs threw up a confounding mystery.
It was a lot lighter than physicists had expected.
With mass and energy interchangeable, the energy of the Higgs field was surprisingly low.
And this meant that supersymmetry became a white knight riding in to save the day.
This is because if ordinary particles have sparticle partners, they would partly cancel each other out leading to a low energy Higgs field.
Add in the ability to explain dark matter and the unification of forces at high energies, and supersymmetry seemed to hold the upper hand.
And yet, that cancellation only works if sparticles are also relatively light.
The heavier they are, the harder it is to use them to square away the lowly mass of the Higgs.
And this was the problem.
The LHC is smashing particles together with such ferocity that it should be producing sparticles at the lighter end of what is possible.
And yet once again, like IceCube and LUX, the silence was deafening.
The jury heard the harsh as loudly as any testimony.
As the prosecution pressed home the advantage, the defense scrambled for explanations.
Maybe light sparticles do exist, but somehow the LHC is missing them.
It's unlikely, but possible.
More likely is that if sparticles do exist, they're too heavy for the LHC to produce at current energies.
But that then makes it nearly impossible for supersymmetry to explain the featherweight mass of the Higgs.
To the jury, it sounded less like confidence and more like backtracking.
For decades, supersymmetry had been the defense's star witness.
Beauty incarnate, the promise that string theory could finally make contact with reality.
Now, that witness looked evasive, its testimony collapsing under cross-examination.
And even that still wasn't the end.
The higher the mass of the sparticles becomes, the harder it is to use supersymmetry to explain the full triumvirate of dark matter, force unification, and Higgs mass.
Physicists are forced to fine-tune the theory with surgical precision, undermining much of supersymmetry's original far-reaching appeal.
And so yet again, when confronted with a deluge of experimental evidence to the contrary, the defense team seems to squirm and wriggle its way out of it.
In an essay aimed at his peers, physicist Mikhail Shifman has urged them to stop developing continued, baroque-like, aesthetically unappealing modifications to supersymmetry.
It's a sharp prosecution argument with familiar sting.
Supersymmetry remains beautiful, but is increasingly edging ever further away from testable ground.
Once more, the defense team was forced to pivot.
Their original alibi, that supersymmetry elegantly explained the Higgs mass, was quietly shelved.
Now, a a theory once operating on the fringes was called to the stand, an idea that came, at least in part, from Nima Arkani-Hamed.
Arkani-Hamed was born in Houston, Texas, 10 days before Apollo 16 touched down on the lunar surface in 1972.
